content: Vitamin K deficiency in newborns can lead to a condition called Hemorrhagic Disease of the Newborn (HDN), which is characterized by bleeding during the first weeks of life. HDN is categorized into three types: early, classic, and late. Early HDN occurs within the first 24 hours after birth and is not addressed in this review. Classic HDN typically occurs between the first and seventh days of life, with common bleeding sites including the gastrointestinal tract, skin, nasal passages, and circumcision wounds. Late HDN occurs between the second and twelfth weeks of life, with bleeding most commonly occurring in the brain (intracranial), skin, and gastrointestinal tract. Vitamin K is routinely administered to newborns as a preventive measure against HDN, but the optimal method of administration remains uncertain. The primary objectives of this review were to evaluate the effectiveness of vitamin K prophylaxis in preventing classic and late HDN and to compare the efficacy of different administration routes. Specifically, the review sought to answer the following questions: Does a single dose of vitamin K given after birth significantly reduce the incidence of classic and late HDN? Is there a difference in effectiveness between oral and intramuscular administration? Can multiple oral doses of vitamin K significantly reduce the incidence of classic and late HDN? The review utilized the standard search strategy of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. It included all randomized or quasi-randomized trials that compared different methods of vitamin K prophylaxis in newborns, as well as trials comparing vitamin K to placebo or no treatment. Data were independently extracted by the authors and analyzed using Cochrane's standard methods, including relative risk, risk difference, and weighted mean difference. Two randomized trials were identified that compared a single intramuscular dose of vitamin K to placebo or no treatment. These trials assessed the effect of vitamin K on clinical bleeding. A single intramuscular dose of vitamin K was found to reduce clinical bleeding during the first seven days of life, including bleeding associated with circumcision. It also improved biochemical markers of coagulation. Eleven additional randomized trials were identified that compared various regimens of oral and intramuscular vitamin K. These trials did not assess clinical bleeding but focused on biochemical markers of coagulation. A single oral dose of vitamin K improved coagulation markers during the first seven days of life. There was no evidence of a difference between oral and intramuscular administration in terms of their effects on coagulation markers. However, plasma vitamin K levels were lower at two weeks and one month in infants who received a single oral dose compared to those who received a single intramuscular dose. In contrast, a three-dose oral regimen resulted in higher plasma vitamin K levels at two weeks and two months compared to a single intramuscular dose. The authors concluded that a single intramuscular dose of vitamin K (1.0 mg) administered after birth is effective in preventing classic HDN. Both intramuscular and oral vitamin K (1.0 mg) improve biochemical markers of coagulation during the first seven days of life. However, neither intramuscular nor oral vitamin K has been evaluated in randomized trials for their effectiveness in preventing late HDN. Additionally, oral vitamin K, whether given as a single dose or in multiple doses, has not been tested in randomized trials for its impact on either classic or late HDN.
